title: Best automotive CRM software: a dealership buyer’s comparison
summary: Compare our automotive CRM with DriveCentric, VinSolutions, CDK, DealerSocket and AutoRaptor using official sources and a practical demo test.
body_markdown:
The best automotive CRM software is the system your dealership can use to move customer opportunities forward: a usable record, a clear owner, the right next action and a reliable connection to the systems that complete the work.


Start your shortlist with **our platform, Clearline, alongside DriveCentric, VinSolutions, CDK CRM, DealerSocket and AutoRaptor** . Each offers automotive CRM capabilities. The surrounding products differ, so compare the package you would buy rather than treating every feature on a vendor website as included.


We publish this comparison and include our platform in it. This is a source-linked buying framework, not an independent award or a hands-on benchmark. Product information was reviewed on **October 26, 2026** . Use the[dealership AI buying guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/pillars/dealership-ai-buying-guide) to connect the shortlist to your store’s requirements.


## Decide whether you need a CRM, a DMS change or another workflow


An automotive CRM manages customer relationships and the work around them: leads, communication, opportunities, stages, tasks and appointments. A DMS handles core dealership operations such as accounting, parts and repair orders. Some providers sell both categories or connect a CRM to a wider retail suite.


An AI communication product can answer and follow up with customers while another CRM remains the place where staff manage opportunities. It may also include its own customer workspace. Ask to see where your team will work every day.


For example, better call coverage does not by itself replace desking, an OEM lead program or a required equity tool. A customer record does not establish accounting functionality. Our[CRM, DMS and customer-data guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/centralizing-customer-data-for-dealerships) explains those system roles in more detail.

## Where each CRM belongs on your shortlist


### Our CRM: customer work across conversations and departments


We link a customer to vehicles, opportunities, tasks, meetings and conversation history. Teams can configure pipeline stages and work from board or table views. Tasks can carry an assignee, due date, department, priority and status.


That makes our CRM worth evaluating when customer work crosses sales, service and BDC. You can enable AI booking, cancellation, rescheduling and inventory jobs with separate permissions and setup. Read the[AI dealership CRM guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/ai-crm-car-dealership) for a customer-to-task walkthrough.


**Check the boundary:** validate desking, OEM requirements, reporting, permissions, import/export and integration scope before deciding whether our platform becomes your main CRM workspace or works alongside existing tools. Our CRM capabilities do not establish a replacement for every retail-suite product.


### DriveCentric: pipeline and communication in the sales workspace


DriveCentric’s Engagement Hub publishes a stage-based pipeline, customer communication history, live inventory visibility, video messaging, mobile tools and performance dashboards. Its page separates the hub from add-ons such as AI agents.


**Check the package:** have the salesperson and manager use the same opportunity, then demonstrate the proposed agents. Confirm what is included rather than pricing the hub and assuming every add-on comes with it.


### VinSolutions: CRM connected to Cox Automotive data and products


VinSolutions presents an automotive CRM with Cox shopper insights, AI and connections to desking and marketing products. Those connections may matter when the dealership’s buying brief includes data and tools from that ecosystem.


**Check the usable data:** ask which shopper signals are available for your store, how they appear in a customer record and what staff can do with them. Confirm the required subscriptions and integration scope.


### CDK CRM: customer workflows within a broader dealership offering


CDK’s CRM page describes lead response, appointment management, a unified customer inbox, AI assistance, writing and summaries, reporting, mobile tools and integrated desking.


**Check the daily work:** have CDK demonstrate the proposed CRM with your current DMS, rather than inferring the integration from a shared provider name. Include staff follow-up, a changed appointment and an incomplete action.


### DealerSocket: CRM with retail and equity requirements


DealerSocket’s CRM and connected product pages describe lead workflows, communication and current AI capabilities. Its[desking](https://dealersocket.com/products/crm/sales/desking/) and[RevenueRadar](https://www.dealer.solera.com/products/dealersocket/revenue-radar/) offerings deserve separate evaluation when deal construction and equity/lifecycle opportunities are part of the brief.


**Check the scope:** identify which products the store depends on today and what a replacement would need to preserve. Our[Clearline vs DealerSocket comparison](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/clearline-vs-dealersocket-crm) covers that decision in more detail.


### AutoRaptor: CRM scope organized around the dealership’s team


AutoRaptor’s pricing page groups plans by user count and lists lead/contact management, communication, action planning, tasking, inventory matching and reports. It also says additional charges may apply to premium integrations.


**Check the complete quote:** use your actual team size, messaging volume and connections. Ask to see a new lead, an assigned task, inventory matching and a manager’s view of outstanding work.


## Give every vendor the same customer journey


A feature checklist becomes useful when you test it against the work your team must complete. Use a test customer and vehicle, with no sensitive production information, and run these steps:


1. **Create the record.** Add contact details and link the relevant vehicle. Show how existing records are found and how duplicates are reviewed.
2. **Open an opportunity.** Choose a pipeline and stage. Assign the staff member responsible for the next action.
3. **Continue the conversation.** Ask about a vehicle or service, then correct a detail. See whether the team can find the updated history.
4. **Create owned work.** Add a follow-up task with a due date. Show where an overdue task appears and how a manager reassigns it.
5. **Book and change a visit.** Confirm a time, then reschedule or cancel it. Inspect the actual appointment record.
6. **Test an exception.** Make a transfer fail or request an unsupported action. Identify who receives the unresolved work.
7. **Inspect the connected system.** Show exactly what was read, created or changed in the DMS or retained CRM.


Record what passed, what required configuration and what remained with a person. A transcript summary and a completed task are different results. A booked appointment and an attended appointment are also different results.


For a fuller acceptance sheet, use the[dealership AI vendor scorecard](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/how-to-evaluate-dealership-ai-vendors) .


## Verify the integration one object at a time


For every connection, identify the source of truth, sync direction, supported fields, update delay, failure handling and extra fees. “Integrates with your DMS” is too broad to answer these questions.


Our[PBS integration](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/clearline-pbs-systems-integration) provides a concrete example. Contacts and vehicles can be off, pull-only or two-way for supported changes. Two-way service appointment sync requires contacts and vehicles to be two-way, with a selected service calendar and OP-code mappings. Workplan events, tasks/reminders and appointments are pull-only.


That distinction matters if staff expect a task created in one workspace to appear in the other. Ask every vendor for the equivalent object-level explanation on your setup.


## Compare price after matching the operating scope


Ask shortlisted vendors to quote the same rooftops, staff, channels, usage, integrations, implementation and contract period. Include products you must retain for desking, equity, phone service or marketing.


Use our[automotive CRM pricing guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/automotive-crm-pricing) and its fill-in worksheet. Public capability lists do not establish a like-for-like price comparison, and the least expensive subscription may leave required work in another paid tool.

## Frequently asked questions


What is the best CRM for a car dealership? +


There is no universal winner. Start with the workflows, integrations and retail tools your store needs. Compare our CRM with DriveCentric, VinSolutions, CDK CRM, DealerSocket and AutoRaptor against the same customer journey and quote scope.


Is automotive CRM software the same as a DMS? +


No. CRM focuses on customer relationships and opportunity work. A DMS runs core functions such as accounting, parts and repair orders. A provider may offer both, but evaluate each requirement separately.


Does an AI CRM replace the BDC? +


That is a staffing decision, not a feature label. Test which routine work AI can complete, then keep clear human ownership for negotiations, exceptions, unresolved tasks and customer relationships.


Can your platform replace an existing automotive CRM? +


We provide native contacts, vehicles, opportunities, pipelines and tasks. Replacement depends on the store’s required retail tools, integrations, permissions, reporting and migration/export needs. A department-specific or alongside deployment may be the appropriate fit.


How should a dealer compare CRM prices? +


Match stores, users, modules, usage, integrations, implementation and contract terms. Request written quotes and separate first-year transition costs from ongoing costs.
